resources.string: ActuA11y demonstrates accessibility patterns in readable source code. Each topic has two versions, switched with the toggle in the app bar: a Naive version built without accessibility in mind, and a Better version built with it. Naive versions are deliberately flawed — if one feels broken, that is the point, not a bug in this app.\n\nIf you use TalkBack, switch access, or a keyboard, try both versions of a topic and compare.
Learn how to use TalkBack (opens Android\'s official documentation)
Images and icon buttons need descriptions so TalkBack can read them aloud.
Turn on TalkBack and swipe through the examples below. Note what — if anything — is announced for each one, then switch versions with the toggle in the app bar and compare.
A smartphone icon representing a mobile device

For meaningful images, pass a non-null string to the Image contentDescription parameter — TalkBack reads it when the image is focused. For decorative images, pass null; Compose removes the node from the accessibility tree entirely.

For icon-only buttons, set contentDescription on the Icon inside IconButton. This is the only name TalkBack has for that button.

See: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties

Neither the meaningful image nor the icon button carries a contentDescription. Compose's Image only adds a semantics node when contentDescription is non-null, so the meaningful image here carries none at all — TalkBack has nothing to focus and skips it silently, indistinguishable from a genuinely decorative image. The IconButton is still a real clickable node, so TalkBack does focus it, but with no name for what it does.

The decorative image is unchanged from the Better version — a decorative image is correctly null in both, so there is nothing to contrast on that element specifically.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties

TalkBack normally reads elements in roughly the order they appear on screen, top to bottom. But when elements overlap — a button floating over the corner of a list, for example — that raw ordering can get confusing, jumping between areas in a way that does not match what the screen looks like.

Turn on TalkBack and swipe through the list and the round button over its corner below. Note the order things are announced in — does it finish the list before reaching the button, or does the button interrupt partway through? Then switch versions with the toggle in the app bar and compare.

The list above carries Modifier.semantics { isTraversalGroup = true }. TalkBack's swipe order is computed by sorting the accessibility tree geometrically, banding nodes into rows by screen position. Where a floating element's bounds overlap another region — as the button here overlaps the list's last row — that geometric sort can interleave the two unless one of them is marked as an atomic group. isTraversalGroup tells the sort to treat this list as a single unit: its own children are still ordered normally within it, but from the outside it behaves as one node relative to the button.

older articles and answers describe this same idea under the name isContainer. That API still compiles today — it is only @Deprecated, not removed — but it is a dead stub: Compose's traversal sort reads only SemanticsProperties.IsTraversalGroup and never looks at IsContainer, so code still using isContainer has no effect on TalkBack ordering even though it builds without error.

See: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.IsTraversalGroup

This list carries no isTraversalGroup, so its rows and the overlapping button are sorted together in a single geometric pass, the same pass used for any sibling whose bounds intersect it.

TODO(verify): confirm on a real device whether TalkBack actually interleaves the button between list rows in swipe order for this exact layout, and record the Compose BOM version and API level tested.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.IsTraversalGroup

Within a group, TalkBack normally reads elements left to right, top to bottom. Sometimes the visual order and the sensible reading order disagree — a dismiss button placed in the top-left corner of a card, for example, usually should not be the first thing announced.
Turn on TalkBack and swipe through the card header below. Note whether the title or the dismiss button is announced first, then switch versions with the toggle in the app bar and compare.
Card header with a dismiss button

Both elements in the header above carry an explicit Modifier.semantics { traversalIndex = … } — 0f on the title, 1f on the dismiss button — so the title sorts first regardless of the button sitting to its left on screen.

Crucially, the Row itself also carries isTraversalGroup = true. traversalIndex only reorders siblings within their nearest enclosing traversal group; without one, it has no effect at all. See the Naive version of this same screen, which sets the identical indices but omits the group.

See: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.TraversalIndex

This header sets the exact same traversalIndex values as the Better version — 0f on the title, 1f on the dismiss button — but the enclosing Row is not marked isTraversalGroup. Per Compose's own documentation, traversalIndex only takes effect within an enclosing traversal group; without one it is silently ignored, and TalkBack falls back to raw left-to-right order, announcing the dismiss button before the title. Nothing here looks wrong when reading the code — the indices are set correctly — which is exactly what makes this mistake easy to miss.

TODO(verify): confirm on a real device that the dismiss button is announced before the title here, and that the Better version announces the title first, recording the Compose BOM version and API level tested.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.IsTraversalGroup

TalkBack users can jump directly between section headings on a screen, skipping everything in between — similar to how a sighted reader\'s eye jumps straight to bold section titles when skimming a page. That only works if a heading is actually marked as one; text that merely looks bold, with no underlying semantics, is invisible to that navigation mode.

Turn on TalkBack, switch its reading control to \"Headings\", and try jumping between the three section titles below. Then switch versions with the toggle in the app bar and compare — the text looks identical in both, but only one version can actually be jumped between.
Manage your sign-in details and linked accounts.
Choose which alerts you receive and how.
Control what data is shared and with whom.

Each section title above carries Modifier.semantics { heading() }, in addition to its bold titleMedium styling. TalkBack\'s \"Headings\" reading control uses exactly this property — not text size or font weight — to decide what counts as a heading, so a user in that mode can swipe directly between \"Account\", \"Notifications\", and \"Privacy\", skipping the body text under each.\n\nSee: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.Heading

These section titles are styled identically to the Better version — same font, same weight, same size — but carry no heading() semantics. Visually they read as headings; to TalkBack's "Headings" navigation they do not exist at all, so a user in that mode finds nothing to jump between and has to fall back to swiping through every line of body text to find a section.

TODO(verify): confirm on a real device that TalkBack's Headings reading control finds zero stops on this screen, versus three on the Better version, recording the Compose BOM version and API level tested.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.Heading

A pane is a visually distinct portion of a screen — a tab\'s content area, the inside of an open drawer — that can change without a full screen navigation. TalkBack has no built-in way to notice a pane\'s content changed unless the app tells it, the same way it is told the screen\'s own name when a topic first opens.

Turn on TalkBack and switch between the two view options below. Note whether anything is announced when the content underneath changes, then switch versions with the toggle in the app bar and compare.

The content pane below carries Modifier.semantics { paneTitle = … }, and that string changes to match whichever view is selected. Per Compose's own documentation, a pane is a visually distinct portion of a window whose appearance or content can change independently — accessibility services can only announce that a pane changed if the pane's title itself changes when its content does. Switching between Summary and Details here never navigates anywhere; the same composable stays on screen throughout.

Contrast this with the paneTitle already set on this screen's own root — that one announces the screen's name once, on arrival, like every topic in this app. This one is expected to fire again on every selection change, which is the distinction requirements draw between "pane titles" as its own topic and the paneTitle every screen already carries.

TODO(verify): confirm on a real device that TalkBack announces the new pane title each time the view switches, and record the Compose BOM version and API level tested.

See: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.PaneTitle

This content pane switches between the same two views as the Better version, with identical layout and text — but it carries no paneTitle of its own, only the screen-level one set once when the topic first opened. TalkBack has no signal that the content underneath changed at all: no announcement, and focus does not move, so a user relying on TalkBack may not realize anything happened after tapping Summary or Details.
